findings.title: Layerzero config file includes 1-of-1 DVN setup
findings.description: The project's LayerZero configuration file (`layerzero.config.ts`) specifies a 1-of-1 DVN (Decentralized Verifier Network) setup, which is significantly less secure than the actual on-chain configuration. The root cause is a discrepancy between the deployment configuration file and the live chain state. Although the on-chain setup correctly uses a 3-of-3 DVN quorum (involving Canary, LayerZero Labs, and Deutsche Telekom), the config file still reflects an outdated and insecure 1-of-1 model. An attacker could potentially exploit this mismatch if the configuration were ever redeployed from source, leading to a single point of failure in message verification. This could allow forged cross-chain messages to be accepted, resulting in unauthorized token minting across chains.

findings.title: No rate limits configured on any peer
findings.description: The deployed OFT contracts lack inbound and outbound rate limiting on peer chains, despite the presence of scripts (`setInboundRateLimit.ts`, `setOutboundRateLimit.ts`) intended to configure them. The cause is the omission of rate limit enforcement during deployment. Without rate limits, a single lzReceive call—once authorized by the 3-DVN quorum—can mint the full 10 billion token supply in one transaction on any chain. An attacker who gains control of a single DVN node or compromises message integrity could exploit this to flood a chain with tokens, causing massive inflation and loss of economic integrity. While the 3-DVN quorum provides some protection, the absence of rate limits increases the blast radius of any successful attack.

findings.title: Inconsistent multisig threshold between EVM chain and Solana chain
findings.description: The ownership and delegate configuration for the OFT contracts uses different multisig thresholds on EVM chains (Base, BNB Chain) versus Solana. On EVM chains, a Gnosis Safe with 4-of-7 threshold is used, while on Solana, a Squads V4 multisig uses a 5-of-8 threshold. This inconsistency creates an operational risk where governance actions requiring multisig approval may succeed on one chain but fail on another due to differing quorum requirements. The root cause is the lack of alignment in multisig configuration across chains. In a scenario where coordinated cross-chain configuration updates are needed, partial approval could lead to inconsistent states, potentially blocking critical upgrades or emergency responses. This undermines the reliability and coherence of cross-chain governance.
